# Preface and Big-Picture Roadmap {.unnumbered}

Welcome to this six-lecture companion course to the [part on affine Toda theory on the half-line](book:sec-boundary-scattering) of the book [Affine Toda field theory](https://gustavdelius.github.io/affine_toda/).

If you open the book's half-line chapters cold, it is easy to feel as though you have walked into a vast cathedral of identities after the scaffolding has been taken down. You meet the boundary Yang–Baxter equation, Sklyanin's double-row monodromy matrix, the discrete sign table $(C_0,\dots,C_n)\in\{\pm 1\}^{n+1}$ of Corrigan, Dorey, Rietdijk, and Sasaki and Bowcock, Corrigan, Dorey, and Rietdijk [@cdrs1994; @bcdr1995], the mirror-image Hirota $\tau$-functions, the Delius–MacKay coideal subalgebras $B_{\hat\epsilon}\subset U_q(\hat{\mathfrak g})$ [@delius_mackay2003], the generalized $q$-Onsager algebras [@baseilhac_koizumi2005; @baseilhac_belliard2010], and pages of fused blocks of trigonometric $\sin$-factors and Barnes double gamma functions. Every theorem is precise, every convention is nailed down, and every check script passes—yet a student learning the subject for the first time inevitably asks:

*Where did these structures actually come from? Why does a boundary break the bulk symmetry in this exact way, and how could I possibly have discovered these calculations with my own chalk and blackboard?*

The purpose of these lectures is to put the scaffolding back up. Rather than surveying every affine Dynkin diagram in encyclopedic breadth, we will go after **depth of understanding and calculational craft**. Throughout all six lectures we will work inside two concrete laboratories where we can carry out the decisive matrix multiplications and linear systems by hand:

1. **The rank-1 laboratory $a_1^{(1)}$** (sine-Gordon and sinh-Gordon), where the soliton multiplet is self-conjugate ($V\simeq\bar V$: the antisoliton lies in the same doublet as the soliton), $2\times 2$ matrices let us see every pole and residue with the naked eye, and a two-parameter continuous family of integrable boundaries exists [@gz1994].
2. **The rank-2 laboratory $a_2^{(1)}$** ($3\times 3$ matrices, where the fundamental representation is complex, $V\not\simeq\bar V$), which is the first place where non-commuting adjacent simple roots meet at the wall. The $a_2^{(1)}$ example exhibits the rigidity of the simply-laced $a_n^{(1)}$ boundaries; other affine types can keep continuous parameters at some nodes [@cdrs1994; @bcdr1995; @delius_mackay2003].

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
These lectures are also available as a [PDF](half-line.pdf).
:::

## The Five Overarching Big Ideas

Everything in the book's half-line part revolves around five conceptual surprises. Keep your eye on these five threads as you work through the lectures:

### 1. The $90^\circ$ Euclidean Trick: The Wall is an Initial State {.unnumbered}

On the full line $x\in\mathbb R$, spatial translations give conservation of momentum $P$, and crossing symmetry comes from rotating a four-point scattering diagram by $90^\circ$ in Euclidean spacetime. Put a wall at $x=0$ and restrict the world to the left half-line $x\le 0$: spatial translation invariance is gone. Yet in Lecture 1 we will follow Ghoshal and Zamolodchikov [@gz1994] and perform that same $90^\circ$ Euclidean rotation, $(x,t_E)\mapsto(\tilde x,\tilde t_E)=(t_E,-x)$, on the half-plane. What was a spatial boundary at $x=0$ existing for all time becomes an **initial state** $|B\rangle$ at $\tilde t_E=0$, across all of space. Because the surviving conserved charges forbid particle production, at nonzero rapidity $|B\rangle$ emits only pairs of particles with opposite rapidities $(-\theta,+\theta)$, weighted by the continued reflection matrix; a particle with a one-point coupling to the boundary can also be emitted alone at zero momentum. A single consistency check on this pair-creation state gives **boundary crossing-unitarity**—a functional equation that mixes the reflection matrix $K(\theta)$ with the *bulk* $S$-matrix $S(2\theta)$ at double the rapidity, because each emitted particle has to cross its partner.

### 2. Higher-Rank Rigidity: Why Continuous Boundaries Freeze {.unnumbered}

In sine-Gordon ($a_1^{(1)}$), you can dial two continuous boundary parameters at $x=0$ without losing integrability [@gz1994]. You might naturally expect $a_n^{(1)}$ ($n\ge 2$) to admit $n+1$ continuous boundary couplings $C_j$. When Corrigan, Dorey, Rietdijk, and Sasaki and Bowcock, Corrigan, Dorey, and Rietdijk [@cdrs1994; @bcdr1995] tested this in 1994–1995, they found a surprise: within Sklyanin's construction with a field-independent reflection matrix, the $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge 2$, boundary couplings cannot be tuned continuously. Every $C_j$ is restricted to the discrete choices $C_j=\pm 1$ (or $C_j=0$ all at once, the Neumann wall). Full Dirichlet conditions $\vec\phi(0,t)=\vec\phi_0$ admit no field-independent reflection matrix in finite-dimensional evaluation representations without trivial summands; the book proves this as its [no-Dirichlet theorem](book:prp-no-dirichlet). We will see this rigidity emerge twice—first classically in Lecture 2 from Sklyanin's double-row Lax pair [@sklyanin1988], where adjacent simple roots fail to commute, and then quantum-mechanically in Lecture 5 from the deformed quantum Serre relations of generalized $q$-Onsager algebras [@delius_mackay2003; @baseilhac_belliard2010].

### 3. Virtual Mirror Solitons and Non-Constant Vacuum Backgrounds {.unnumbered}

How does a nonlinear soliton bounce off a wall at $x=0$? In Lecture 3 we will see that the half-line Hirota equations are solved by a **virtual mirror soliton** that comes in from the unphysical region $x>0$. Saleur, Skorik and Warner found this method of images for sine-Gordon [@ssw1995], and Delius extended it to affine Toda theory [@delius1998a]. Parity conjugates the Hirota species, so for the boundaries considered there the mirror construction returns a soliton of species $a$ as its **antisoliton** $\bar a = n+1-a$. The phase shift of the virtual collision with the mirror, which takes place behind, at or in front of the wall depending on the boundary, becomes the physical reflection time delay $\Delta t(\theta)$. When we continue from imaginary coupling to real-coupling affine Toda particle theory ($\beta\to -i\beta$), the mirror construction survives: a *stationary* soliton–antisoliton mirror pair at zero rapidity gives explicit regular, non-constant static backgrounds $\vec\phi_{\rm vac}(x)$, on the allowed intervals of its modulus, for boundaries at which $\vec\phi=0$ is no longer a solution [@bowcock1998; @delius_gandenberger1999]. They are believed, but not proved, to be ground states, and the construction does not cover every sign pattern.

### 4. Why Coideal Subalgebras Replace Hopf Subalgebras {.unnumbered}

In the bulk, nonlocal conserved charges generate the quantum affine algebra $U_q(\hat{\mathfrak g})$ [@bernard1991], whose coproduct $\Delta(Q) = Q\otimes 1 + \Theta(Q)\otimes Q$ has a built-in left–right asymmetry because the topological tail sits exclusively to the left of the charge density. On the half-line $x\le 0$, charges leak into the wall at $x=0$. In Lecture 4 we will run boundary conformal perturbation theory [@gz1994; @delius_mackay2003] and watch the two anomalous boundary surface terms cancel against a topological tail term, leaving, to first order in the boundary coupling, a conserved linear combination
$$
b_j = e_j + q_j^{-1} f_j k_j + \hat\epsilon_j k_j .
$$
Its exact conservation is then taken as the defining property of the boundary symmetry. When we take the coproduct of $b_j$, it does *not* land in $B_{\hat\epsilon}\otimes B_{\hat\epsilon}$—so $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ is not a Hopf subalgebra! Instead, because the boundary sits at the rightmost end of the spatial ordering $x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_N < 0$, the coproduct lands in $U_q(\hat{\mathfrak g})\otimes B_{\hat\epsilon}$. That asymmetric algebraic structure is a **left coideal subalgebra** (the quantum symmetric pairs of Letzter and Kolb [@letzter1999; @kolb2014] are the corresponding right coideals, related to these by an automorphism that reverses the coproduct), and it turns the quadratic boundary Yang–Baxter equation into a purely *linear* intertwining equation $K(\theta)\pi_\theta(b_j) = \bar\pi_{-\theta}(b_j)K(\theta)$.

### 5. The Proposed Classical–Quantum Dictionary and Weak–Strong Boundary Duality {.unnumbered}

When we put the classical story (Lectures 2–3) next to the quantum coideal story (Lectures 4–5), a puzzle appears. First-order boundary conformal perturbation theory around the Neumann wall ($C_j=0$) suggests $\hat\epsilon_j=0$, whereas the $a_n^{(1)}$ coideal intertwiner exists only for $\hat\epsilon_j=0$ (diagonal $K$) or for the non-zero value $\hat\epsilon_j^2 = \epsilon_*^2 = \frac{1}{4\cos^2(\pi\omega/2)}$ (non-diagonal $K$), with all nodes of the same kind (proved for $a_2^{(1)}$ in Lecture 5; the book checks $n\le7$ and sketches the general case). And why does real-coupling affine Toda theory have $2^{n+1}$ sign choices $C_j=\pm 1$ classically, when explicit regular vacua, from $\vec\phi=0$ or from mirror pairs, are known only for patterns with $\prod_j C_j = +1$, and from $a_3^{(1)}$ on not even for all of those? In Lectures 5 and 6 we examine the book's proposed dictionary between boundary conditions and coideals. We compute breather reflection factors by boundary fusion, continue them to real coupling ($\omega\to -2/B$), and compare their classical limits with the classical reflection factors. The resulting proposed amplitudes for the uniform boundary ($C_j\equiv +1$, $\hat\epsilon_j=0$) and the Neumann boundary ($C_j\equiv 0$, $\hat\epsilon_j = +\epsilon_*$) are exchanged exactly by $B\leftrightarrow 2-B$. This **weak–strong boundary duality** was proposed by Corrigan in rank one and conjectured by Gandenberger for $a_2^{(1)}$ and by Delius and Gandenberger for $a_n^{(1)}$ [@corrigan1998; @gandenberger1999a; @delius_gandenberger1999]. Identifying the amplitudes with the boundaries rests on the continuation and on a choice of CDD factor, so it remains conjectural. The book supplies numerical semiclassical evidence; these lectures do not perform a WKB calculation.

## Syllabus of the Six Lectures

| Lecture | Title & Core Theme | Book chapters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lecture 1** | **The Wall at $x=0$ and the $90^\circ$ Euclidean Trick.** Half-line conservation laws, the three reflection equations (S/K, braid, and soliton-conjugating), the boundary state $|B\rangle$, boundary crossing-unitarity, boundary bound states, and the reflection factors of boundary scaling Lee–Yang. | [Boundary scattering](book:sec-boundary-scattering) |
| **Lecture 2** | **Sklyanin's Double Row and the Rigidity of Higher-Rank Boundaries.** The affine Toda boundary action, Sklyanin's double-row monodromy matrix $\mathcal T(\lambda)$, the classical reflection equation, why $a_1^{(1)}$ is continuous while $a_2^{(1)}$ is restricted to $C_j\equiv0$ or $C_j=\pm 1$, and why changing $\sigma=T$ to $\sigma=\dagger$ unlocks Delius's soliton-preserving wall. | [Boundary conditions](book:sec-boundary-conditions) |
| **Lecture 3** | **Mirror Solitons, Time Delays, and Non-Constant Vacua.** Parity conjugation of Hirota $\tau$-functions, virtual collisions with mirror solitons, exact classical time delays $\Delta t(\theta)$, continuation to real coupling, stationary-soliton vacuum backgrounds, the missing-vacuum puzzle, and linearized wave reflection. | [Solitons on the half-line](book:sec-half-line-solitons) |
| **Lecture 4** | **Boundary Nonlocal Charges, Left Coideals, and Sine-Gordon.** Boundary OPEs and the double-pole contact identity, why the boundary at the right of $x_1<\dots<x_N<0$ forces a left coideal $\Delta(B)\subset U_q(\hat{\mathfrak g})\otimes B$, solving the linear intertwining equation for Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov's $K(\theta)$, fixing the physical sign of $q$, and boundary bound states from 1D $B$-modules. | [Boundary sine-Gordon](book:sec-boundary-sine-gordon), [boundary quantum groups](book:sec-boundary-qg) |
| **Lecture 5** | **The $a_2^{(1)}$ Intertwiner Puzzle and Generalized $q$-Onsager Algebras.** Solving the $3\times 3$ soliton-conjugating intertwiner for $a_2^{(1)}$, the $2\times 2$ determinant that forces $\hat\epsilon_j\in\{0,\pm\epsilon_*\}$, proving the deformed quantum Serre relation and its Cartan obstruction, Letzter–Kolb quantum symmetric pairs vs. $q$-Onsager algebras, and how a non-analytic normalization could hide $\epsilon_*$ from first-order perturbation theory (a conjectural argument). | [Boundary quantum groups](book:sec-boundary-qg), [soliton reflection](book:sec-soliton-reflection), [quantum symmetric pairs](book:sec-qsp) |
| **Lecture 6** | **From Solitons to Breathers, Real-Coupling Particles, and Duality.** Soliton scalar factors and their CDD freedom, boundary fusion onto the singlet breather $B_1$, continuation $\omega\to -2/B$, the proposed uniform–Neumann weak–strong duality $B\leftrightarrow 2-B$, solitonic boundaries, the $a_2^{(1)}$ boundary bound-state tower $b_{n,m}$ with its rotor-like diagonal states $b_{n,-n}$, and a boundary Coleman–Thun diagram whose naive double pole is reduced by a zero. | [Boundary sine-Gordon](book:sec-boundary-sine-gordon), [soliton reflection](book:sec-soliton-reflection), [particle reflection](book:sec-particle-reflection) |

## How to Study with These Notes

Every lecture is built around two pedagogical devices:

- **Blackboard Calculations (`### Blackboard Calculation ...`):** Whenever a decisive result arrives, we stop speaking in generalities and work out the calculation on the blackboard in our $a_1^{(1)}$ or $a_2^{(1)}$ laboratory, step by step. Where a long computation is taken from the book instead, the text says so. Read these with pen and paper in hand.
- **Guided Rediscovery Exercises (`## Guided Rediscovery Exercises`):** At the end of each lecture you will find three multi-part, scaffolded exercises that guide you step-by-step to rediscover key identities, special limits, or higher-rank generalizations for yourself, with intermediate checkpoints so you never get lost in a sign or prefactor.
- **Verification and Figure Scripts:** The scripts in `code/lectures/` check selected formulas and numerical examples and generate the figures. Their PASS results apply to the assertions they actually implement; they do not verify every displayed derivation, exercise, source attribution or physical interpretation. Each lecture says what its script checks. Click any inline script path to inspect or run the code yourself.
